concepts.name: Article 368: Scope, Limitations, and Constituent Power
key_dimensions: Whether Article 368 confers constituent power or merely defines procedure — Sankari Prasad vs. Golak Nath debate
Distinction between 'law' under Article 13 and 'constitutional amendment' under Article 368
24th Amendment Act inserting 'notwithstanding anything' clause to override Golak Nath verdict
Basic Structure Doctrine as an uncodified but judicially enforced limitation on Article 368 power

concepts.name: Simple Majority Amendments: Provisions Excludable from Article 368
key_dimensions: Constitutional provisions amendable by simple majority of Parliament outside the purview of Article 368 — often misidentified as ordinary legislation
Key examples: admission of new states (Article 2), formation of new states (Article 3), Second Schedule, Official Languages (Part XVII), quorum, salaries of MPs
UPSC trap: These are constitutional changes but NOT amendments under Article 368 — critical distinction
Abolition or creation of Legislative Councils under Article 169 as another simple majority example requiring state legislature's non-binding resolution

concepts.name: Special Majority Under Article 368(2): Two-Thirds Plus Absolute Majority
key_dimensions: Dual requirement: 2/3rd majority of members present and voting AND absolute majority (more than 50%) of total membership of each House
UPSC trap: Both conditions must be simultaneously satisfied — failing either invalidates the amendment
Distinction from ordinary special majority (e.g., Rajya Sabha's Article 249 resolution requiring only 2/3rd of members present and voting)
Scope: Applies to most fundamental rights, DPSP amendments, federal provisions not requiring ratification

concepts.name: Special Majority Plus State Ratification: Federal Entrenchment Provisions
key_dimensions: Third and most stringent category: Special majority in Parliament + ratification by not less than half of state legislatures

Exhaustive list of provisions requiring state ratification — Article 54, 55, 73, 162, 241, Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, Chapter I of Part XI, Seventh Schedule lists, representation of states in Parliament, Article 368 itself
UPSC trap: State legislatures ratify by simple majority — no special majority required at state level; no time limit prescribed for ratification
No provision for state legislature to withdraw ratification once given — judicially untested but academically settled

concepts.name: Rajya Sabha's Equal and Mandatory Role in Constitutional Amendments
key_dimensions: Unlike ordinary legislation, Rajya Sabha cannot be bypassed in constitutional amendments — no joint sitting provision under Article 368
UPSC trap: Joint sitting (Article 108) is NOT applicable to constitutional amendment bills — Rajya Sabha has absolute veto
Significance of bicameral equality in amendment procedure as a federal safeguard
Contrast with Money Bills and ordinary bills where Rajya Sabha's power is limited or overridable

concepts.name: Presidential Assent to Constitutional Amendment Bills: Mandatory vs. Discretionary
key_dimensions: Post-24th Amendment: President has NO discretion — must give assent to constitutional amendment bills (Article 368(2) proviso amended)
Pre-24th Amendment position: President could withhold assent — Golak Nath context made this a contested area
UPSC trap: Contrast with ordinary bills where President can withhold assent or return — constitutional amendment bills cannot be returned
No pocket veto possible for constitutional amendments unlike ordinary bills

concepts.name: Golak Nath Case (1967): Parliament's Amending Power and Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: 11-judge bench ruling: Parliament cannot amend Part III (Fundamental Rights) — amendment is 'law' under Article 13(2)
Doctrine of prospective overruling applied for the first time in India — previous amendments to FR saved
Political fallout leading to 24th Amendment (1971) directly overruling Golak Nath
UPSC trap: Golak Nath was overruled by Kesavananda Bharati — understand the timeline: Golak Nath (1967) → 24th Amendment (1971) → Kesavananda (1973)

concepts.name: Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): Basic Structure Doctrine
key_dimensions: 13-judge bench (largest ever): Parliament can amend any part including Fundamental Rights but CANNOT destroy the 'basic structure'
Basic structure elements identified — supremacy of constitution, republican/democratic form, secularism, separation of powers, federal character, judicial review, rule of law, unity/integrity
Article 368 amended by 24th and 25th Amendments partially upheld, partially struck down — 55 clause-wise voting creates interpretational complexity
UPSC trap: Basic structure is NOT defined in the Constitution — it is a judge-made doctrine; its elements are not exhaustive and continue to evolve

concepts.name: 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976): Scope and Judicial Reversal
key_dimensions: Called 'Mini-Constitution' — most sweeping amendments: added 'socialist', 'secular', 'integrity' to Preamble; added Fundamental Duties; made DPSP override FR
Added Article 368(4) and (5) claiming amendments are beyond judicial review — subsequently struck down in Minerva Mills
UPSC trap: Added Tenth Schedule? No — Tenth Schedule was added by 52nd Amendment (1985); common confusion
Emergency provisions made more draconian — partly reversed by 44th Amendment (1978)

concepts.name: Minerva Mills Case (1980): Harmony Between Fundamental Rights and DPSP
key_dimensions: Struck down Article 368(4) and (5) inserted by 42nd Amendment — judicial review of amendments is itself part of basic structure
Restored balance between FR (Part III) and DPSP (Part IV) — neither can completely override the other
UPSC trap: Parliament's unlimited amending power is itself unconstitutional — the limitation (basic structure) is a basic structure element
Distinction from Kesavananda: Minerva Mills clarified that removing limitations on amending power destroys basic structure

concepts.name: Doctrine of Basic Structure: Elements and Evolving Judicial Interpretation
key_dimensions: Core elements consistently recognized: Supremacy of Constitution, Sovereign democratic republic, Secularism, Separation of powers, Federalism, Judicial review, Free and fair elections, Rule of law
Contested/evolving elements: Right to equality (IR Coelho), Parliamentary democracy, Judicial independence (NJAC judgment 2015)
UPSC trap: 'Harmony and balance between FR and DPSP' is basic structure (Minerva Mills) — not just FR or DPSP individually
NJAC judgment (2015) — striking down 99th Amendment applying basic structure to collegium system — most recent significant application

concepts.name: Waman Rao Case (1981) and IR Coelho Case (2007): Ninth Schedule and Basic Structure
key_dimensions: Waman Rao: Laws added to Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) are immune from FR challenge; post-1973 additions are subject to basic structure test
IR Coelho (9-judge bench 2007): Reaffirmed Waman Rao — any Ninth Schedule law violating basic structure of FR can be struck down regardless of when added
UPSC trap: Ninth Schedule does NOT provide blanket immunity — it is conditional on basic structure compliance post-1973
Significance: Right to Property (Article 31) was deleted from FR — Ninth Schedule was the primary vehicle to protect land reform laws

concepts.name: Preamble: Amendability and Its Status as Part of the Constitution
key_dimensions: Berubari Case (1960): Preamble is NOT part of the Constitution — cannot be used for interpretation
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Overruled Berubari — Preamble IS part of Constitution and can be amended under Article 368
42nd Amendment (1976): Added 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' — only amendment to Preamble ever made
UPSC trap: Preamble can be amended but its basic features (sovereign, democratic, republic) are arguably part of basic structure — unamendable in substance

concepts.name: Seventh Schedule: Amendment of Three Lists and Federal Implications
key_dimensions: Seventh Schedule (Union List, State List, Concurrent List) requires special majority PLUS state ratification — highest protection category
Parliament can legislate on State List subjects under Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 but cannot unilaterally shift entries between lists without amendment procedure
UPSC trap: Abolition of State List or transferring entries to Union List permanently requires ratification — but temporary Parliamentary legislation on State List subjects does NOT amend the Schedule
Historical shifts: Entry 92C (Service Tax) added to Union List by 88th Amendment; subsequently subsumed under GST (101st Amendment)

concepts.name: 101st Constitutional Amendment: GST and Cooperative Federalism in Amendment Context
key_dimensions: Required state ratification as it amended Seventh Schedule — altered taxation entries in all three lists
Created Article 246A (concurrent power to levy GST), Article 279A (GST Council) — new federal institution created by amendment
UPSC trap: GST Council's decisions are recommendatory — not binding — settled by Supreme Court in 2022 (Union of India vs. Mohit Minerals)
Demonstrates how amendment procedure itself can reshape federal financial relations — significant for federalism questions

concepts.name: 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978): Reversal of Emergency Excesses
key_dimensions: Restored several provisions diluted by 42nd Amendment — strengthened fundamental rights during Emergency
Deleted Right to Property from FR (Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31) — made it only a legal right under Article 300A
UPSC trap: Article 20 and Article 21 made non-suspendable even during Emergency — this was 44th Amendment's crucial addition (not original Constitution)
Raised bar for national emergency proclamation — requires cabinet's written advice; Lok Sabha can revoke by simple majority

concepts.name: 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985): Anti-Defection and Tenth Schedule
key_dimensions: Added Tenth Schedule — disqualification on grounds of defection; amended Articles 101, 102, 190, 191
Originally Speaker/Chairman was final authority — Kihoto Hollohan Case (1993): Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review; also held Tenth Schedule does NOT violate basic structure
UPSC trap: 91st Amendment (2003) amended Tenth Schedule — merger provision changed from 1/3rd to 2/3rd; individual member cannot claim split protection anymore
Kihoto Hollohan also held that Schedule itself required state ratification (as it amended legislative body provisions) — paragraph 7 (finality clause) was struck down

concepts.name: 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992): Federalism Extension and Amendment Significance
key_dimensions: Added Parts IX and IX-A — constitutionalized Panchayati Raj and Urban Local Bodies; added Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules
UPSC trap: These amendments create a 'third tier' but do NOT create a federal unit — states retain control; subjects in 11th and 12th Schedule are not mandatory transfers
Amendment route required as new Parts and Schedules were added — required special majority but NOT state ratification (no Seventh Schedule change)
Contrast: Gram Sabha mentioned in Constitution for first time (Article 243A) — but its powers defined by state legislature, not Constitution

concepts.name: Procedure for Introducing Constitutional Amendment Bills: Parliamentary Mechanics
key_dimensions: Can be introduced in EITHER House of Parliament — unlike Money Bills which must originate in Lok Sabha
UPSC trap: Can be introduced by private member OR government — no restriction; but in practice only government introduces
Must be passed separately by each House — no provision for joint sitting (unlike ordinary/financial legislation)
After passage by both Houses and state ratification (where required), presented to President — no option to return; assent is mandatory

concepts.name: Comparison of Indian Amendment Procedure with Other Constitutions: Flexibility vs. Rigidity
key_dimensions: K.C. Wheare's classification: India's Constitution is 'predominantly rigid' with some flexible elements — three-tier amendment procedure reflects this hybrid
Comparison with USA: Much harder to amend (2/3rd Congress + 3/4th states); India's procedure relatively easier explaining frequency of amendments (over 105)
Comparison with UK: Completely flexible — Parliament can change any constitutional convention; India's entrenchment of basic structure makes it uniquely rigid in substance
UPSC angle: India has been amended 106 times (as of 2024) — more than any other written constitution — yet basic structure doctrine prevents fundamental character change
